item.title: Trump Heads to Ireland for the Irish Open at His Golf Course
item.description:
President Trump was heading to Ireland on Friday for a weekend at his golf resort, after two days spent trying to energize Republicans to turn out in the midterm elections in November.

The president will attend the Irish Open golf tournament, held at his Trump International Golf Links & Hotel in County Clare. Some diplomatic business will be included in the trip: He is expected to speak with President Catherine Connolly, who has criticized U.S. and Israeli foreign policy, and with Micheál Martin, the prime minister.

The trip to Ireland comes as the Republican Party faces an uphill battle to keep control of Congress in the midterm elections, which are a little more than 50 days away.

Mr. Trump has become more engaged with Republicans’ prospects as the elections get closer. He just spent two days in Dallas imploring people to vote for Republicans, and dangled a promise to send every American adult $5,000 if Republicans keep control of the House and Senate. Next week, he is traveling to North Carolina to campaign for a Republican Senate candidate, Michael Whatley.

But his efforts on behalf of Republicans often come on his own terms, and in ways that do not necessarily align with what the party wants. Mr. Trump can seem focused on his own projects — whether it is his golf club in Doonbeg, his White House ballroom or building a towering arch in the nation’s capital.The White House declined to comment.

Various polls have found that voters feel Mr. Trump has the wrong priorities. And in recent weeks, Republicans have expressed concern that Mr. Trump should be spending more of his political war chest on Republican candidates in tough races.

In an interview with Fox News, Mr. Trump said he did not intend to campaign as vigorously for congressional Republicans as he had for his own campaign. Asked if he would campaign harder than ever, Mr. Trump said “no.”

“The hardest I ever campaigned, because I had to win, was the last,” he said of his own race. “I took four months, no empty days, no empty hours.”

Asked if the midterm elections were not just as important as his own race, Mr. Trump said, “It’s never as important. Look, I’m campaigning for other people.”

Mr. Trump’s trip also comes at a moment when he and his party are facing blowback about high prices for groceries and gasoline amid the conflict with Iran, which is grinding on with no clear endgame.

Critics say it is a bad look.

“He can’t be bothered to care about economic concerns of the American people but when it comes to the Trump family business, he’s ready to take a trip and go to Ireland for a golf tournament,” said Sarah Matthews, a deputy press secretary in Mr. Trump’s first term. “This just shows where his priorities lie.”

Past presidents have also faced criticism for frequently leaving the White House for getaway weekends or golf trips.

President Joseph R. Biden Jr. left the White House most weekends to spend time in Delaware with his family. The Obama administration was on the defensive when President Barack Obama traveled to Martha’s Vineyard to golf in 2014 amid various crises, including killings by the Islamic State in Iraq and Syria.

One of the more frequent critics of Mr. Obama’s travel at the time was Mr. Trump.

“Can you believe that, with all of the problems and difficulties facing the U.S., President Obama spent the day playing golf,” Mr. Trump said on social media in 2014. “Worse than Carter.”

Brendan O’Leary, an Irish political scientist and professor at the University of Pennsylvania, said that there is usually not much downside to a trip to Ireland for American presidents, particularly given the tens of millions of Irish American voters.

“If you conduct your foreign trips with an eye to the home electoral market, there’s no harm in having a nice trip to Ireland,” Mr. O’Leary said.

But Irish Americans no longer vote as a bloc, he said, and Mr. Trump is deeply unpopular in Ireland, where videos of protests are as likely to be the images associated with the trip as his meeting with Mr. Martin.

“The risk is, of course, that the Irish may not like you,” Mr. O’Leary said. “And it is very palpably clear that the bulk of the citizens of Ireland do not think well of Trump.”

item.title: Republicans, Facing Midterm Peril, Try to Brand Democrats as Communists
item.description:
One by one, Republican speakers at President Trump’s midterm convention in Dallas this week turned to a far-fetched argument with echoes of the Cold War.

Speaker Mike Johnson of Louisiana claimed, “Next year the communists will be in Congress — that’s what’s so frightening.” Representative Steve Scalise of Louisiana, the No. 2 House Republican, said implausibly that there had been a “Bolshevik Revolution in the Democrat Party.”

And when Mr. Trump, the ringleader of this new Red Scare, took the stage, he returned — again and again and again — to baseless claims that Democrats were running as communists in the midterms.

“It’s going to be a communist country if they win,” he predicted, one of at least 60 times a speaker at the convention mentioned communism or communists.

Although this year’s Democratic primary season brought a surge of left-wing momentum, and a handful of victories by democratic socialists running for Congress in Colorado, Michigan, New York, Pennsylvania and Florida, no credible midterm candidate identifies as a communist. And there is little momentum behind any communist movement in U.S. politics at the federal level.

Still, for months now, Mr. Trump and Republicans, staring down a daunting political environment and the potential loss of one or both houses of Congress, have been trying to cast Democrats as communists, deploying a charge that has little overlap with Democrats’ actual platforms.

Republicans have been grasping for a potent attack line as they confront widespread voter discontent with the president’s war with Iran as well as high gasoline and grocery prices. They believe the left-wing congressional nominees have offered an opening to build an argument that Democrats are outside the mainstream.

“Stalin. Mao. Castro. Democrats,” the Republican National Committee wrote on social media last month. “Different leaders, same goal.”

Whether the attacks make a difference in the midterms is still far from clear. Some Democrats have expressed worry that the rise of democratic socialism in their party could play into Republican efforts to cast them as extremists and that constant mentions of communism could blur the lines for some voters. At the same time, Mr. Trump’s overheated language could weaken the force of the argument.

Mr. Trump and Republicans have pointed to a series of victories by democratic socialists in Democratic primary races — including a suite of June results in deep-blue New York and a stunning Senate upset last month in conservative-leaning Florida — to accuse their opponents of harboring radical beliefs.

Perhaps not since the 1950s or ’60s has an American political party spent so much time talking about communism. In Mr. Trump’s telling, communism poses the gravest danger to the country. It is more severe, he says, than World War I, the Japanese raid on Pearl Harbor in 1941 or the Sept. 11 attacks in 2001.

Communists, he said in a bizarre aside at a July rally in Georgia, even want to destroy an American landmark.

“They tried taking Mount Rushmore down — they want to blow it up,” he claimed, without elaborating.

In some ways, far-left leaders have fed the argument. In 2020, Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, a leader of the progressive movement and a self-described democratic socialist, praised elements of the Communist Cuban revolution. And Darializa Avila Chevalier, a democratic socialist who unseated a Democratic congressman in a New York primary in June, once maintained a social-media account that circulated a post suggesting that public libraries should carry more Marxist literature.

Two days after Ms. Avila Chevalier and two other self-described democratic socialists swept House primaries in New York, a group of centrist House Democrats signed a letter declaring, “We are capitalist, not socialist.”

Representative Don Davis, a centrist Democrat running for re-election in a battleground district in North Carolina, said in an interview that he had signed the letter because voters across his district had been expressing anxiety about communism.

“I have heard it from the northernmost portions of the district to the central all the way to the southernmost portions of eastern North Carolina,” he said. “Without any doubt, yes, there are genuine concerns.”

By the time the left-wing wave crashed into Florida last month, with the victory of the democratic socialist Angie Nixon in the Democratic primary for Senate, more lawmakers and the veteran Democratic strategist James Carville had agreed to sign the letter, too.

Most Americans have unfavorable views of socialism, according to polls. Communism polls much worse. And even as Mr. Trump mislabels Democrats as communists, some Democrats have jokingly blurred the lines themselves, referring to the area of New York City where one democratic socialist House candidate won as the “Commie Corridor.”

Jon Fleischman, a former executive director of the California Republican Party, said that “your options are limited when the president’s ratings on a lot of key issues, most notably the economy, are underwater.” But he added that describing Democrats as communists was “smart” strategically and would “freak out people.”

Hillary Clinton told Kara Swisher on the “Pivot” podcast that Republican messaging accusing Democrats of being communists would be “very effective” politically. She said Republicans had most likely tested it before making it their central attack.

“People on the left have to be prepared to answer that,” Mrs. Clinton said.

The deployment of over-the-top warnings about communism has become a staple of Mr. Trump’s speeches.

“These are not mere political disagreements like differences over taxes or regulations,” Mr. Trump said in a dark speech at Mount Rushmore the weekend of July 4, referring to communism more than a dozen times. “Communism is a mortal threat to American liberty. It is the greatest threat to our country, including World I, World War II, Pearl Harbor or even 9/11.”

Republicans have enhanced their standing with Hispanic voters in Florida by linking left-wing American leaders with authoritarian communist governments in Latin America, said former Representative Carlos Curbelo, a Florida Republican. But Mr. Curbelo was skeptical that the president’s claims of communism would be as potent with other voters.

Representative Don Bacon, a Republican from a swing Nebraska district who is retiring, said democratic socialists were a “good group to run against.” But he questioned the president’s approach of labeling them as communists.

“When you throw out the labels, people don’t know if it’s true or not,” Mr. Bacon said. Mr. Trump might be better off highlighting left-wing Democrats’ policy positions or inflammatory past statements, the congressman added: “I would quote these guys.”

Some Democrats say Republicans are embracing a straw-man argument.

Brad Lander, a self-described democratic socialist from Brooklyn who beat a Democratic congressman in a primary in June, said democratic socialists had “in many cases” been the “fiercest opponents of communists.”

“Democratic socialists want an extension of democracy into more parts of working people’s lives,” he said.

Even as Mr. Trump rages against the far left and seeks to tie it to communist governments, his administration has moved to expand the bounds of executive power — drawing accusations from Democrats that the president has more in common with autocratic communist leaders than they do.

The Trump administration has also been unusually aggressive in acquiring ownership shares of private companies, securing stakes in dozens of companies and reaching a deal that gave the government extraordinary influence over U.S. Steel.

And after Mr. Trump this week floated sending $5,000 to every adult American — but only if Republicans keep their congressional majorities in the midterms — some fiscal hawks in his party criticized what they said was a socialist-style gimmick.

Mr. Trump’s decision to speak so frequently and forcefully about communism is a throwback to the Cold War, said Barbara A. Perry, a presidential scholar at the University of Virginia. No president since George H.W. Bush has focused on communism in any meaningful way, she said.

Mr. Trump was a child during the so-called Red Scare, a period of political paranoia in the 1950s. In that era, Senator Joseph McCarthy, a Wisconsin Republican, led a series of investigations into supposed communist influence in the U.S. government.

Mr. Trump rose to prominence as a real estate developer in the 1970s and 1980s, when tension between the United States and the communist Soviet Union was high.

The president’s renewed focus on communism is in line with his long-running focus on the 1980s. Roy M. Cohn, Mr. Trump’s mentor and lawyer during that period, had decades earlier been chief counsel to McCarthy’s Senate investigations into communism. Those investigations became infamous for their overreaches.

Mr. Trump’s claims of an internal communism threat, rather than an external one, are particularly reminiscent of the Red Scare of the 1950s, Ms. Perry said.

Representative Jamie Raskin, a Maryland Democrat, said Mr. Trump wasn’t qualified to lecture Democrats about communism, pointing to the president’s tendency to embrace President Xi Jinping of China, who leads his country’s Communist Party, and Kim Jong-un, the authoritarian leader of North Korea.

Mr. Trump has celebrated his “good relationship” with Mr. Kim, saying that they “fell in love” during his first term and that the North Korean leader had sent him “beautiful” letters.

Mr. Trump has said he plans to meet again with Mr. Kim by the end of the year.

Taylor Robinson contributed reporting.

item.title: Why Finding Jimothy Is Really About Finding Ourselves
item.description:
He has no neck.

That’s what stopped the internet in its tracks: a raccoon whose head sits directly on his shoulders. A raccoon who runs without appearing to travel, loping in the manner of a man crossing a hot parking lot in flip-flops.

His name, if you’re one of the few who haven’t heard, is Jimothy. He lives in my part of Seattle, and that’s as precise as I’ll get. Nobody around here wants the world clogging our street corners, hoping for a glimpse. Which hasn’t, however, stopped me.

On the evening of July 13, Kiana Hall saw something moving under a parked car near her home. A cat, she thought. Then it stepped into the light. She got a few seconds of video and uttered what remains the best single line spoken on this subject.

“What am I looking at?”

She posted it to her friends, saying that she and her husband had been blessed by a Jimothy. Why Jimothy? To her, he just looked like one. Nobody has come up with anything better.

By morning, her video was ricocheting worldwide. Within a week, it had racked up 10 million views and media from Germany to the Philippines to New Zealand were calling Ms. Hall. Soon, Jimothy was the subject of a mural, tattoos at a shop up the street, a cryptocurrency, a charity auction that raised $271,975 for a food bank and an honorary degree from the University of Washington.

Seattle City Council members declared this Jimothy Summer. The Seattle Mariners held Jimothy Night, doling out baseball cards of the raccoon, including a single gold-bordered edition that a 13-year-old fan sold on eBay for over $20,000.

Jimothy received no royalties. He was up a tree.

Jimothy isn’t the first. Every so often, a town reaches into its animal population, pulls one out, endows it with a name, personality and opinions and takes it in like an orphan. Then social media churns, and out comes a bona fide world celebrity.

Professionals have thoughts about the phenomenon. Aimee Frazier is a licensed counselor who practices ecotherapy, which means her clients get the woods, not the couch. She explains the pattern as a reaction to the way people live their lives now. Every building, every street was built by humans for humans, Ms. Frazier said, adding: “We’re so humancentric.”

A hobbled raccoon under a Prius is a reminder that the arrangement is recent. “He pulls us out of ourselves,” Ms. Frazier said, and back into something people have lost touch with.

Some of these animals we take in out of pity. Consider Pedals, the New Jersey bear who couldn’t use his front paws and walked upright past the trash like a neighbor getting the paper. For the many humans who fear their flaws could subject them to scorn, here was an animal whose disability was the narrative — and he became a hero.

Then there are wayward ones: Flaco, the eagle-owl loose on Manhattan’s Upper West Side, or P-22, the cougar who zigzagged across Los Angeles freeways to live under the Hollywood sign. They refused the rules, thumbed a paw or a claw at the system, proving the metropolis, its permits and codes and bumper-to-bumper grind are escapable.

What’s Jimothy? A bit of everything. He’s damaged, unbothered, in the wrong place and pulling it all off without noticing.

If Jimothy came when called, he would be a pet, and a pet is of no special use to a city. The whole lore runs on the animal’s indifference. In a world where everyone seems to be working an angle, people fall in love with something that won’t look up when asked.

Sometimes my neighborhood seems like a zoo. Bald eagles land in the tall trees, scanning for rabbits. Coyotes come in packs, famished and ready to pounce. Raccoons? They’re hardly strangers — though they usually don’t get fan clubs and bumper stickers.

Oscar Velasco-Schmitz, a friend down a few blocks, recently saw two gangs of raccoons duking it out in a late-night brawl. They battled across his trees and the neighbor’s roof. The sound is seared in his mind. “A cacophony WrestleMania throwdown!” is how he described it.

There was a small one getting worked over while another hung on for dear life, Mr. Velasco-Schmitz recalled. Was it Jimothy? Maybe, he said, but he sure hoped not.

None of these animals consent to being the objects of our fascination, and they’re often the ones who pay. Norway shot the walrus Freya because people wouldn’t stop crowding her for selfies. New Yorkers fought to keep Flaco free, and then he died after striking a building with a gut full of rat poison.

A short time ago, somebody spotted Jimothy in the neighborhood again. Another video flew across the digital ether. There he goes, prancing down a street strewn with browned Seattle leaves. “Jimothy is alive and well,” read the post, which was met with 75,000 likes. That’s where this is now — a terrible dread takes over if Jimothy isn’t seen for a few weeks.

These days, I drive slower down my street. Not only for his sake. In this era of social media malice, imagine the harrowing fate of the driver unfortunate enough to run over Jimothy.

One evening I spotted four or five raccoons in the cypress tree a few feet from my front door. They stared at me with the blunt disinterest of people waiting for a city bus.

My only thought: Get the dang dog inside!

My dog Chana is the reason I’m out on these blocks at night. Against Jimothy, Chana might have a puncher’s chance. Cornered by Jimothy’s mother — full-sized, full-necked, unnamed and unproclaimed — he’d be raccoon appetizer.

So when Chana gets up at 3 a.m. to relieve himself in the backyard, unleashed, we watch or listen for the bark. Lately I’ve been listening for coyotes, too, on behalf of a raccoon I’ve never seen. He has no neck.

item.title: How Trump Is Wielding Power to Stifle Speech
item.description:
The Justice Department has sent F.B.I. agents to reporters’ homes to serve subpoenas and, in at least one case, flashed a warrant to seize devices. The Pentagon has fired the editor and publisher of its traditionally independent newspaper, Stars and Stripes, and blocked access to other journalists who refused to sign pledges that would limit their reporting.

Regulatory agencies are using their powers to pressure media organizations over their content. The administration has stripped funding from public television and radio. Angry over stories he does not like, President Trump has sued major news organizations and the White House has taken control of the previously independent press pool that tracks the president, deciding which outlets can participate.

Almost 20 months into Mr. Trump’s second term, his long-running media clashes have grown into a sweeping campaign to control speech in America that stands out for applying so many levers, so fast, all at once.

Driven by personal pique, fury over leaks and a determination to shape the political narrative to his advantage, Mr. Trump is deploying the might of the federal government and filing personal lawsuits — targeting not just journalists and liberal critics, but also comedians and talk show hosts, and the corporate entities behind them.

To the president and his allies, he is simply demanding accountability for what he casts as biased, unfair and sometimes inaccurate coverage and criticism — an effort that has been welcomed by longtime conservative press critics like those at the Media Research Center.

Aides noted that the White House has this year expanded who gets invited to cover events, such as the off-the-record presidential lunch with network anchors that precedes the annual State of the Union address.

In a statement, White House Communications Director Steven Cheung said that “biased reporting from the media is a disservice to the American people,” adding: “We utilize every tool available to ensure that accurate reporting is provided to the public and the stain of those who knowingly peddle false information is held accountable.”

Free speech advocates say the president’s intent is apparent: to punish, intimidate and silence dissenters.

“There’s not a week that goes by where they’re not taking a new step to curtail press freedom in the country,” said Clayton Weimers, the executive director of the North America division of Reporters Without Borders. “We have measured a substantial diminishment of press freedoms.”

When challenged in court, the president and the administration have frequently lost, confronted with strongly worded rulings from judges affirming First Amendment rights.

Still, even the path to legal victory can have severe financial and reputational costs for those he views as adversaries, which have included The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal and the BBC. And each time the president assails what has long been considered protected speech, media analysts say, he is eroding norms and undercutting the role of an independent press.

Reporters Without Borders maintains an index that tracks press freedom in 180 countries, clocking governmental threats, subpoenas and the vindictive use of regulations against journalists. The United States now ranks at its lowest since the organization started the index in 2002 — 64th, just above Panama and just below Botswana. The trend is the same at similar indexes kept by the Freedom of the Press Foundation and the V-Dem Institute of Sweden.

There is a long record of U.S. presidents taking steps to curtail speech. President Woodrow Wilson imposed strict censorship and forced dissenting publishers out of business during World War I. Richard M. Nixon kept an enemies list, and his aides threatened F.C.C. action against broadcasters. More recently, the George W. Bush White House expanded government secrecy and the Obama administration went after the sources of journalists through leak investigations.

Mr. Trump had inveighed against the Biden administration for what he and his supporters portrayed as draconian pressure on social media companies to censor disfavored content often at their expense, promising at his second inauguration to “stop all government censorship.”

Now his administration is breaking new ground in stifling dissent with personal lawsuits and novel uses of executive power, longtime First Amendment lawyers say, with implications that extend far beyond Mr. Trump’s presidency.

“We live in a different world under this administration because the threats are so grave,” said Floyd Abrams, who has worked on free speech cases for 60 years. “It’s one thing to say there’s an extraordinarily powerful First Amendment, but unless and until courts rule on these matters, the threat is very real.”

Long before he took office, Mr. Trump was well known for his media feuds. As a developer and reality TV star, he was quick to threaten defamation suits against those who challenged his assertions about his business successes and his wealth.

Mr. Trump has been candid about his aim: to inflict pain, even if it was fleeting. After bringing a failed libel suit against the former Times reporter Timothy L. O’Brien, whose book “TrumpNation” estimated Mr. Trump to be worth far less than he claimed, the president gloated about forcing the publisher to spend money. “I did it to make his life miserable, which I’m happy about,” he said.

In his first term, the president branded journalists as “fake news” and crudely attacked reporters, especially women.

In his second term, Mr. Trump is now imprinting his pugilistic approach across the machinery of the federal government. Those who once might have checked him have been replaced by loyalists who often use their power to fulfill Mr. Trump’s desire to punish perceived enemies.

Soon after his inauguration, the White House banned The Associated Press from the Oval Office and Air Force One, ostensibly because the wire service would not call the Gulf of Mexico by Mr. Trump’s preferred name, the Gulf of America. Another reason for the ban: The A.P. would not give the Trump team rights to its photo of Mr. Trump, bloodied with a raised fist, after he was shot in Butler, Pa., in 2024. At a private lunch with Mr. Trump and network anchors last year, White House aides tied the A.P. ban to the denial of the rights to the photo, according to two people briefed on the event.

Mr. Trump’s team is unapologetic about its goal of achieving firmer control over the national information environment — what Mr. Cheung, the communications director, has dubbed in a social media post, “Full Spectrum Dominance.”

Brendan Carr, the chairman of the Federal Communications Commission and one of the most aggressive supporters of Mr. Trump’s efforts, has said that the president is “reshaping the media landscape.”

Citing the big broadcast networks, Mr. Carr told an interviewer for CNBC last year that “for years government officials just allowed those entities, with executives sitting in Hollywood and New York, to dictate the political narrative.” Mr. Trump, he added, has “fundamentally changed the game.”

One of the Trump administration’s strategies appeared to take root in a dispute between Elon Musk and the liberal press watchdog group Media Matters for America.

In 2023, Mr. Musk was furious about a Media Matters article that showed pro-Nazi posts were running on his social media platform X alongside promotional posts from major consumer brands, contributing to an advertiser exodus from the site.

A longtime Trump adviser, Stephen Miller, took to X to pointedly note that Republican state attorneys general had the power to consider civil and criminal fraud charges against the group. In short order, Mr. Musk sued Media Matters for allegedly manipulating the X algorithm to produce its results, the Texas attorney general’s office opened an investigation into deceptive trade practices and the Missouri attorney general followed with its own inquiry.

Media Matters won court injunctions blocking the Texas and Missouri investigations. But soon after Mr. Trump took office again, the Federal Trade Commission, newly headed by the conservative lawyer Andrew Ferguson, began its own investigation, demanding internal documents related to Media Matters’ methodology for evaluating media sources and its finances.

The investigation was part of a broader F.T.C. inquiry into whether several groups that work to identify online disinformation were colluding with advertising firms to direct money away from disfavored outlets. Conservatives saw the issue as central to what some labeled a “censorship industrial complex.”

A federal judge in Washington ultimately determined that the F.T.C.’s investigation of Media Matters presented “a straightforward First Amendment violation.”

But the fight was costly for Media Matters. In addition to paying legal fees, the group said it had self-censored articles to avoid further scrutiny from the agency. (It is still defending itself against Mr. Musk’s suit.)

The F.T.C. also investigated NewsGuard, a site that rates the reliability of online information. It is avowedly nonpartisan in its approach; Fox News, for instance, rates above MS NOW.

In court papers, NewsGuard said it drew attention in part because it had given a low rating to the conservative site Newsmax, which is run by an ally of Mr. Trump’s, Chris Ruddy. Mr. Ruddy had complained that ad agencies were relying on NewsGuard ratings to withhold money from right-leaning outlets like his.

The F.T.C. took another tack that NewsGuard said affected it directly, related to the merger of two of the country’s largest advertising holding companies, Omnicom and Interpublic Group. The F.T.C. entered into a consent decree with the newly joined company barring it from broadly using ratings like those published by NewsGuard to withhold ad spending from certain sites, among other things. (It could still follow individual clients’ requests to do so.)

In a lawsuit filed in February, NewsGuard said the provision effectively placed it on a blacklist, immediately causing it to lose business.

The F.T.C. ultimately dropped its investigations into both NewsGuard and Media Matters, saying it had achieved its goal of defending free speech through agreements with ad firms. It said it was fulfilling its mission of protecting consumers from anticompetitive behavior that “distorted the marketplace of ideas,” as Mr. Ferguson put it.

Dan Schneider, vice president for free speech at the conservative watchdog group Media Research Center, described the actions by the F.T.C. and the F.C.C. as a correction against abuses under the past two Democratic presidents. “Please, let’s not forget history and rewrite everything that went on before,” Mr. Schneider said.

But Rebecca Kelly Slaughter, a Democratic F.T.C. commissioner fired by Mr. Trump last year, said in an interview that the agency’s actions were “a perversion of the F.T.C.’s authorities in order to punish the speech of perceived enemies and reward perceived allies.”

Much of the administration’s action has been led by Mr. Carr. The longtime F.C.C. lawyer is known to frequent the president’s golf clubs when Mr. Trump is there on weekends and often speaks to the president directly about his grievances with news outlets, according to people briefed on their conversations.

He has bent the F.C.C. to the president’s will, investigating the major broadcast networks by reviving largely dormant rules, like those against so-called news distortion — meant to punish the deliberate staging or distortion of a news event. Mr. Carr has also pursued networks for their diversity, equity and inclusion practices, inquiring whether they violate federal law and agency regulations, a tactic the administration has used to significant effect against universities and law firms.

Early on, Mr. Carr extracted extraordinary concessions from Skydance, the company run by the studio executive David Ellison, the son of the billionaire Trump ally Larry Ellison, as it sought to purchase Paramount, the parent company of CBS. To secure F.C.C. approval for the merger, Skydance agreed to end CBS’s diversity policies and appoint a monitor for news bias. (Mr. Trump has since shown a rooting interest in the Ellisons’ attempt to buy Warner Bros. Discovery, which owns CNN.)

Critics, among them F.C.C. chairs from past Republican administrations, have said Mr. Carr is exceeding his authority. Mr. Carr says he is simply following the law by requiring broadcasters to serve the public interest in ways that he says his predecessors had failed to do.

Mr. Trump is clearly pleased with Mr. Carr’s effort to solve the so-called fake news problem, as he put it in a speech in April at a private White House event ahead of the celebrations for America’s 250th anniversary.

“He’s keeping these crooked networks honest,” Mr. Trump said as he spotted Mr. Carr in the crowd, describing his appointee as “the most powerful man in the world.”

After Mr. Trump recently called for punishment of the NBC host Kristen Welker for reporting he did not like, and suggested F.C.C. action against the airing of “fake polls,” Mr. Carr responded by saying the agency was considering “a lot of actions,” including on “fake polls.”

No network has borne the brunt of the president’s ire as much as the Disney-owned ABC network.

Mr. Trump’s animus against ABC grew in 2024, when he sued over the anchor George Stephanopoulos’s characterization of the verdict in the defamation case brought by E. Jean Carroll, who accused Mr. Trump of sexual abuse. ABC settled the suit for $15 million.

In the president’s second term, his anger has increased as the ABC late-night comic Jimmy Kimmel has made him the regular butt of jokes.

Last year, the F.C.C. opened an investigation into the network’s diversity and inclusion hiring policies and revived a conservative group’s complaint over ABC’s 2024 presidential debate.

Early this year, the agency sought to require its talk show “The View” to follow so-called equal-time rules for political candidates, even though the F.C.C. previously agreed that the show qualified for an exemption.

In April, after Mr. Trump and the first lady demanded ABC fire Mr. Kimmel over a joke he made about her being an “expectant widow,” the F.C.C. started an early review of the federal licenses that ABC stations need to operate, years before they are set to expire.

The agency had never brought such a mass challenge to a major network’s station licenses. It said it was doing so because ABC was deficient in its responses to the diversity and inclusion inquiry.

ABC is now fighting the agency’s actions, which it called “deeply un-American.”

The network has asked a federal court to intervene immediately, arguing that Mr. Carr was effectively using the agency’s enforcement process to wage a “retaliatory campaign” that is already negatively affecting its programming decisions.

Out of fear of retaliation, ABC decided to carry live online a prime-time speech that Mr. Trump gave on election security, which it would not have otherwise done, and avoided certain bookings and video clips on “The View,” the network said in court papers.

It also reported onerous F.C.C. demands for documents, including staff communications from inside “The View” and internal ABC News editorial policies.

“It’s unprecedented to seek these records because they are part of the editorial decision-making,” Anna Gomez, the lone Democratic F.C.C. commissioner, said in an interview. “It’s all a strategy, and tools, to intimidate broadcasters into submission.”

Mr. Carr has called ABC’s suit meritless. This month, the F.C.C. moved to get the case dismissed, arguing ABC was simply trying to short-circuit an agency investigation while exaggerating harms to its speech rights.

Trevor Timm, the executive director of the Freedom of the Press Foundation, a nonprofit group that tracks press freedom violations in the United States, said that the administration’s moves “have certainly risen to the level where they’re kind of off the charts.”

Government efforts to subpoena journalists and chill their reporting through threats are at the highest level since the foundation started tracking incidents in 2017.

And as a private citizen, Mr. Trump has filed lawsuits against a wide range of targets including the Guardian newspaper, the journalist Bob Woodward and the Pulitzer Prize board — legal battles often financed by his donor-funded political action committee.

Many of the moves have also drawn stern rebukes and concern from judges.

That was the case after the F.B.I. served a search warrant in January at the home of a Washington Post reporter and seized several of her devices, as part of an investigation into a contractor’s handling of classified material. In February, Judge William B. Porter chastised the government and forbade officials from immediately reviewing the reporter’s materials, saying to do otherwise would be “the equivalent of leaving the government’s fox in charge of The Washington Post’s henhouse.”

While weighing a suit Mr. Trump has personally brought against The Des Moines Register for a poll it published showing him behind in Iowa in 2024, a judge worried that allowing the suit to proceed could have “a massive, chilling effect.”

After a judge harshly questioned government lawyers in July over subpoenas for phone records and testimony from Times journalists who reported on the security capabilities of the new Qatari-donated Air Force One jet, the Justice Department withdrew the subpoenas.

At the time, David McCraw, the paper’s top newsroom lawyer, called the outcome, “an important affirmation of our country’s commitment to a free press,” but added in a statement that the subpoenas “should never have been issued in the first place.”

In siding with The Times in a challenge to restrictions for reporters at the Pentagon, Judge Paul Friedman of U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia wrote in March, “Those who drafted the First Amendment believed that the nation’s security requires a free press and an informed people and that such security is endangered by governmental suppression of political speech.”

After The Times initially prevailed in court, Pentagon officials sidestepped the ruling to again limit the access of journalists to the building. The Times sued again. This time, an appellate panel allowed a key new restriction to stand, at least temporarily — reporters must have escorts inside the Pentagon where they once roamed freely.

The rule remains in place while the legal fight presses on.

item.title: Alabama Is Set to Execute a Murderer. The Jury Wanted Him to Live.
item.description:
A jury in Alabama heard harrowing testimony about a bungled pawnshop robbery in 1998 that quickly turned to bloodshed: Jeffery Lee, 21, charged in with a sawed-off shotgun and opened fire. The store’s owner, hit in the chest and arm, and his ex-wife, who was shot point-blank in the face, were killed. A clerk was wounded; she played dead until Mr. Lee fled.

Jurors voted unanimously to convict him. But when it came to deciding whether Mr. Lee should be put to death, most of the panel opted instead to sentence him to life in prison without parole.

And yet, nearly three decades later, Mr. Lee is on death row, his execution just days away.

Mr. Lee’s case is a relic of an era when judges had the power to override a jury’s sentencing decision, a practice forbidden in Alabama since 2017. He is one of more than two dozen inmates whose death sentences came from judges, not juries.

“We’re still here,” said Mr. Lee, now 49, speaking by phone from death row in Atmore, Ala. “The guys are still here fighting for their lives.”

I have reported on Mr. Lee’s case since the spring, when his legal team succeeded in raising doubts about the constitutionality of nitrogen gas as an execution method. Alabama was ready to put Mr. Lee to death using the gas in June, and had already moved him to the death chamber, when the U.S. Supreme Court intervened.

Mr. Lee agreed to an interview this month after the state rescheduled his execution for Sept. 17, this time using lethal injection.

His case has tangled with some of the most fraught questions hanging over capital punishment in Alabama. In the interview, he discussed how such a sprawling and philosophical debate in society — about the morality of the death penalty and the constitutional boundaries of cruel and unusual punishment — had such direct implications on his fate.

Now that he faces a grim countdown, Mr. Lee talked about what distracted him (blasting worship music) and brought some comfort (Bible verses like Psalm 91). He also focused his frustration on how his sentence was reached, saying that his crimes merited a severe punishment, but that it should be the punishment the jury agreed to.

“I’m not free — that’s punishment,” Mr. Lee said. “And that’s something I’ve been living with for the past 26 years. No way, not one day has been easy.”

Officials in Alabama — which has long had the highest number of death sentences per capita in the country — have resolved to push ahead with executions, even as they wrestle with the legacy of old flawed policies and as limited access to lethal injection drugs has prompted a search for new methods.

And in Mr. Lee’s case, those officials have defended the death sentence as just. “There is absolutely no question as to his guilt,” Steve Marshall, Alabama’s Republican attorney general, said in a statement. “Anything short of carrying out the sentence imposed by the court falls short of justice for the victims, and that is not what victims of this state deserve.”

Still, prominent legal and political figures in Alabama — including some Republicans who are generally supportive of the death penalty — have demanded clemency for Mr. Lee.

Alabama had been the last state to allow judges to override a jury’s sentencing decision before it changed the law with overwhelming bipartisan support in 2017. At some points, one-fifth of the inmates on death row had been sent there using judicial override. Legislative efforts to apply the change retroactively have failed, creating what critics regard as an alarming imbalance.

“When a state concludes that a sentencing practice was unjust — unjust enough to abolish by statute — it ought to reckon with the sentences that practice produced,” Drayton Nabers Jr., a former chief justice of the State Supreme Court and a Republican, wrote in an essay published in June in newspapers across the state.

During the sentencing phase of Mr. Lee’s trial in 2000, his family members testified about his struggles with substance abuse starting from a young age, which precipitated erratic and troubling behavior.

The victim’s relatives and others described the anguish unleashed in Dallas County, a rural and impoverished stretch west of Montgomery, part of a region known as Alabama’s Black Belt primarily for its rich soil.

Helen King, the clerk and surviving victim, shared the torment that had endured long after she called for help. “I still can’t sleep at night, I slap at my kids for no reason,” Ms. King said during the sentencing hearing. “It turned my life upside down.”

Efforts this week to reach Ms. King and relatives of Jimmy Ellis, the store owner, and Elaine Thompson, his ex-wife, were unsuccessful.

Mr. Lee was originally sentenced to die by electrocution, long the state’s primary method before lethal injection supplanted it in 2002. In 2018, as major pharmaceutical companies restricted the sale of the drugs used in lethal injections, Alabama legalized nitrogen hypoxia. The state paused executions for three months in 2022 after botched lethal injection attempts.

Mr. Lee agreed to be executed by nitrogen hypoxia, in which a person breathes pure nitrogen through a mask. Supporters of the method had presented it as efficient and potentially painless.

“We were led to believe that it would be something constitutional, something that wouldn’t involve suffering,” Mr. Lee said of why he chose nitrogen gas.

But after Alabama put the method in place in 2024, witnesses described seeing inmates writhing and gasping for air for 10 minutes or longer.

In a legal challenge to nitrogen hypoxia, Mr. Lee suggested being put to death by a firing squad would be quicker and less cruel. A federal judge agreed. Four .30-caliber bullets aimed at his heart, the judge wrote, “significantly reduces a substantial risk of severe pain.”

Alabama officials countered that the state did not have the legislative approval or the protocol prepared for a firing squad, much less “five expert marksmen willing and able to serve as executioners.”

Mr. Lee’s legal team contends that his agreement to be executed using nitrogen gas included language that prevented him from being put to death by lethal injection. The same federal judge rejected that argument in July.

Since June, Mr. Lee said, he has been caught between relief, as the day he believed could be his last turned out not to be, and dread, as he realizes a last-minute intervention is less likely this time around. He tries not to think about it.

Instead, Mr. Lee, who trained as a minister in prison, said he was leaning once again on the faith that had carried him throughout his time on death row.

“When I stop and choose to focus on what’s going on, I get stuck there,” he said. “I choose each and every day to wake up and not be fearful and afraid.”

Susan C. Beachy contributed research.

item.title: High Prices Spoil Trump’s New Push to Save G.O.P. Majority
item.description:
With less than two months until the midterm elections, President Trump commenced a final push this week to preserve his Republican majority in Congress, arguing that the United States under G.O.P. control had brought prices “way, way down.”

But for many families and businesses, the economy appeared to be on far shakier footing by Friday. Fuel prices soared, mortgage costs climbed and inflation registered uncomfortably high, testing the public’s patience with Mr. Trump’s frequent assurances that the country is on the right track.

The contrast underscored the political and economic stakes for Mr. Trump, who may soon face the wrath of an electorate long spurned by promises in Washington to lower the cost of living. As November draws closer, prices have risen under the president’s leadership, driven largely by an agenda that has included two years of punishing trade brinkmanship and a prolonged war with Iran.

The consequences were evident in the latest gauge of the Consumer Price Index, released on Friday. The report showed that prices rose at an annual pace of 3.4 percent in August, which increased the odds of the Federal Reserve’s raising interest rates next week.

The data came on the same day that a separate, long-running survey from the University of Michigan found that consumer sentiment dropped sharply this month. In that report, Americans expressed new worries that the economy was sputtering, and that inflation would continue to rise.

The unease set the stage for Mr. Trump’s renewed push this week to make the case to voters that he has helped, not hurt, the economy. Over two days of speeches at his party’s midterm convention in Dallas, the president labored to convince Americans that Republicans had achieved “tremendous economic success.”

But Mr. Trump did not limit himself to a brash defense of his record. The president also said he would send a $5,000 check to American citizens if Republicans retained the House and Senate in November, though he has failed to deliver on similar promises in the past.

“So if the Republicans win, you win with us,” Mr. Trump said, soon after adding: “Congratulations. Now all we have to do is win.”

The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

For Mr. Trump, the fight with inflation has proved so pernicious that it has overshadowed even the few bright spots in the economy. Despite nearly two years of policy tumult, the labor market has remained strong, the economy is growing and the country is witnessing a boom around artificial intelligence, one that has generally delighted financial markets.

But those positives have not always been obvious or tangible to voters, who have suffered through years of compounding costs that peaked during the coronavirus pandemic. Those financial strains continued into August, when prices rose faster than hourly wages on a year-over-year basis for the fifth straight month.

“The economy is performing well, but this isn’t buoying consumer attitudes,” Oren Klachkin, the financial market economist for Nationwide, wrote in an analysis of the new inflation data on Friday. “Rather, they’re squarely focused on rising prices and interest rates eating into purchasing power.”

In an interview, Mr. Klachkin added that he did not see inflation “coming down at a meaningful pace any time soon.” He cited a range of risks, including uncertainty around the tariffs in Mr. Trump’s trade war and the war with Iran.

Both of those conflicts worsened this week, a period that was not captured in the latest inflation report. But Americans still felt the consequences. The return to hostilities in Iran, for example, sent the price of Brent crude, the global benchmark, to $110 per barrel briefly on Friday.

It was the first time since July that oil prices had reached those levels, and in the United States, it coincided with a continued surge in gas prices. Nationally, gas averaged nearly $4.30 per gallon by Friday, according to AAA — well over a dollar more than a year ago. Still worse was the cost of diesel, which topped $6 per gallon, setting a record that could deeply affect shipping and transportation.

The increase prompted Kevin Hassett, the director of the White House National Economic Council, to acknowledge that soaring diesel costs in particular represented a “big, big issue” for the economy. In a Friday appearance on Fox Business, he pointed to geopolitical uncertainty — including in the Middle East — as the root cause.

But there was no sign this week that the war with Iran was close to finished. Even Mr. Trump acknowledged at one point that high oil and gas prices could persist until “right after the election,” though he predicted costs would fall quickly, contrary to warnings from economists.

“They’re going to be tumbling down, and we’ll get them down. I think for gasoline, we’ll get them below $2 a gallon,” the president told reporters, adding: “I think it’s going to take a little bit longer than the midterm.”

The renewed energy shock created more headaches for the Fed and its new chairman, Kevin M. Warsh. As the Fed eyes a rate increase to bring inflation into check, Mr. Trump has redoubled his demands for significant rate cuts. Absent a steep reduction, the president even threatened last week that he could cut off all trade with countries that sell more to the United States than they buy. Rates are now in a range of 3.25 to 3.75 percent.

On Wall Street, the economic headwinds also helped to push up the cost of the government’s own borrowing all week. That came in the form of higher yields, which topped 4.9 percent on 10-year bonds, the highest level seen since 2023.

The rise carried significant implications, particularly for homeowners, since mortgage rates closely track yields on those bonds. The average rate on a 30-year loan reached around 6.8 percent last week, according to Michael Fratantoni, the chief economist at the Mortgage Bankers Association, a 15-month high.

At the start of the year, Mr. Trump had promised an aggressive plan to lower housing costs. Since then, a confluence of factors has sent mortgage rates skyrocketing, and led Mr. Fratantoni to predict on Friday that it could reach “at or above 7 percent” soon.

So, too, did high yields raise the costs for Washington to service its own debts, which recently surpassed $40 trillion under Mr. Trump. But an attempt by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to buy up old bonds this week failed to push down yields, as markets shrugged off the intervention.

Brett Loper, the executive vice president for policy at the Peter G. Peterson Foundation, which supports deficit reduction, attributed the poor reception to the many “tectonic forces at play,” including the fast-growing U.S. debt.

Add to that Mr. Trump’s new sales pitch to voters, promising $5,000 to Americans if Republicans prevail in the midterms — a plan that Mr. Loper estimated could cost $1.2 trillion.

That price tag, on top of existing fiscal woes, would probably “lead to greater inflation and higher interest rates,” he said.

]]>

item.title: As Millions of Birds Migrate, Residents Are Asked to Turn Off the Lights
item.description:
By Ishani Desai

More than 300 million birds are expected to soar across the United States on Saturday during their annual fall migration, prompting requests for residents to turn off or dim lights to help ensure their safe flight.

Hundreds of species of birds, such as blackpoll warblers, chimney swifts and scissor-tailed flycatchers, will fly from the Northern Hemisphere to South America for a warmer climate filled with more food, said Dylan Osterhaus, a postdoctoral research assistant at Purdue University who studies migratory birds.

“It’s always like Christmas morning, going out each morning and seeing what new presents arrived from the north,” he said.

But the trek can be dangerous.

At least one billion birds die each year after crashing into skyscrapers and other lighted buildings, said Adriaan Dokter, a research associate who leads Cornell University’s BirdCast, an online resource that tracks the birds in real time.

The birds, which typically travel after darkness falls, will be most heavily concentrated in eastern Minnesota and Michigan on Saturday.

The birds could fly through Illinois and Indiana and then cluster in the Southern states before soaring out of the country, according to projections from the Aeroecology Lab at Purdue University.

Some cities, such as Minneapolis and Chicago, ask residents to turn off or dim lights so the birds do not mistakenly fly toward lit structures.

Building owners or managers could switch off exterior decorative lighting and floodlights and install automatic motion sensors, the Audubon Society said. The lighting should be turned off or reduced from 11 p.m. to 6 a.m.

The leading cause of death for wild birds is crashing into buildings, said Jessica Wilson, the executive director of the NYC Bird Alliance.

Some birds become disoriented during bad weather and can fly into tall buildings. Some migrators also are drawn into well-lit areas and cannot see glass, Dr. Dokter said.

The fall migration, which began in mid-August, could peak over next two weeks, with more than 500 million birds dotting the Northern Hemisphere, Dr. Osterhaus said. The migration period typically ends in mid-November.

The birds rely on weather patterns to determine when to fly, Dr. Dokter said. They can halt their migration if storms settle over a region.

The bird projections studied by researchers at Purdue and Cornell rely on weather radar data, Dr. Osterhaus said.

Certain weather conditions, such as favorable wind shifts, have correlated to instances in which large flocks of birds take off, he said.

Scientists have combined decades of this weather data and built a predictive model to project how many birds will be flying based on how the weather shifts, he said.

Each species has its own migration pattern.

Some species, such as the dark-eyed junco, nest in Canada and then fly in the winter to the United States, Dr. Osterhaus said.

“These birds are really trying to maximize their survival and fitness,” he said.

Generally, the fall migration contains more birds because the summer’s breeding season has concluded, said Catherine Quayle, the communications director for the Wild Bird Fund, a nonprofit that rehabilitates injured or sickened birds and other animals.

From Sept. 5 until Friday, the Wild Bird Fund admitted 453 birds, of which 124 had crashed into windows, she said. The birds cannot tell the difference between a real tree and the reflection of a tree.

In New York City, more than 250,000 birds die each year after crashing into buildings, Ms. Wilson said.

Residents can help by sticking films with patterns on windows to make the glass less clear, Dr. Dokter said.

Alexandra E. Petri contributed reporting.

]]>

item.title: Republican Groups Rush to Paxton’s Aid in Texas After Staying on Sidelines
item.description:
A major Republican group booked more than $51 million worth of advertising in the Texas Senate race on Friday to help Ken Paxton, the G.O.P. nominee whose tight race has become a growing concern in the party as it seeks to keep control of the upper chamber of Congress.

For months, top Republican outside groups stayed away from Mr. Paxton’s contest, where polls show a close competition between him and a well-funded Democratic opponent, James Talarico. But a flood of outside money suddenly arrived over the last two weeks to help Mr. Paxton amid Mr. Talarico’s rising prospects of winning.

The new $51 million investment from Texas PAC, a group affiliated with the Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC allied with Senate Republican leaders, adds to the more than $23 million that has already been booked by a half dozen other G.O.P. groups on advertising for Mr. Paxton from Sept. 1 through Election Day. That gives Mr. Paxton and Republican allies a 5-to-1 spending advantage over Mr. Talarico and Democratic allies, according to AdImpact, a media tracking firm. For months, the Democratic side had possessed a clear spending advantage.

The approximate total of $75 million doesn’t include all of a $10 million Texas ad buy disclosed by President Trump’s super PAC last week or the $2 million-plus investment in voter contact work from Elon Musk’s super PAC.

That Mr. Paxton is abruptly in this position is a twist in the Texas race. After defeating Senator John Cornyn in the primary, with Mr. Trump’s help, Mr. Paxton spent months as a heavy financial underdog, with various Republican groups hoping that at least one would step up to spend in an expensive state that can drain an organization’s coffers. Now, the Republican financial establishment appears to have decided to jump in together to boost Mr. Paxton.

When the Senate Leadership Fund outlined its spending plans in April, an investment in Texas was notably omitted. Pressure to spend mounted from fellow Republicans for months. Alex Latcham, the head of the Senate Leadership Fund, said on Friday that its ad buy “affirms our commitment to maintaining the Republican majority.”

When Mr. Paxton defeated Mr. Cornyn, who some Republicans argued was the stronger general election option, many in the party braced for a more difficult and expensive general election. Allies of Mr. Cornyn, who is close with many donors and served in Senate leadership, were embittered by the outcome, complicating Mr. Paxton’s path to consolidating support. Some wondered why they should have to rescue a candidate they saw as flawed and didn’t want to nominate in the first place.

Buying ads is a fluid process, and campaigns and outside groups often adjust their spending as Election Day nears.

Mr. Talarico, a state representative, is one of his party’s strongest fund-raisers this election cycle and may be able to keep up financial parity without outside help. He outraised Mr. Paxton by a huge margin through the middle of this year, bringing in more than $54 million in 2026 compared with his Republican rival’s nearly $4 million.

From June through August, Mr. Talarico and his allies outspent Mr. Paxton and his by a 7-to-1 margin, according to AdImpact data. During that period, neither candidate had much outside help.

But now pressure will most likely mount on the main super PAC backing Senate Democrats, the Senate Majority PAC, to invest in the state as Republicans now have. The New York Times reported in July that the Senate Majority PAC had given other Democrats the impression that it planned to spend there, even though it, like Republicans until now, has conspicuously avoided Texas.

On Friday, Lauren French, a spokeswoman for the PAC, said, “We’ll continue to watch the race closely, but if you ever needed a sign Paxton was in trouble, this is it.”

item.title: Crashing a Plane for Clicks: Influencers Push Shock Content to Get Views
item.description:
In 2021, Trevor Jacob, a former U.S. Olympic snowboarder, flew a 1940 Taylorcraft plane far above the hills of Los Padres National Forest in Southern California and made a decision he would spend years wishing he could undo.

Cameras he had mounted to record his flight for an online audience captured him announcing that the plane had engine trouble before he bailed out.

A camera attached to a selfie stick he held recorded him parachuting safely to the ground, while cameras fixed to the plane captured it slamming into a hillside.

He posted a 13-minute video on YouTube titled “I Crashed My Plane,” which amassed some five million views. As it turned out, it was a confession.

Federal investigators later determined that the plane had never malfunctioned: Mr. Jacob had staged the crash, hoping for online fame.

The attention was fleeting.

The stunt eroded his life and led to a federal prison sentence.

Mr. Jacob is among a growing number of social media influencers who push the boundaries of safety and good taste in the quest for views, experts said.

Influencers, sensing that the algorithms reward extreme content over routine videos, are navigating this landscape, one where outrage, fear and awe hold viewers’ attention a little longer than tamer fare.

Gone are the years when internet fame was within reach for a teenager filming dance routines in a bedroom, or a parent teaching recipes from a kitchen.

Attention is currency, and sometimes it’s costly.

Across the world, aspiring influencers trespass on skyscraper roofs. They block highway traffic. They provoke strangers in grocery stores, airports and malls. They dangle from helicopters, cranes, trains and cliffs for clips lasting only seconds.

Some are arrested. Others are hospitalized. And, in tragic cases, some have died.

Psychologists who study this field are not surprised.

“As the tech has evolved and influencers stand to earn fame and wealth, it is probably not surprising that some people are willing to risk prison or even death,” said Kaveri Subrahmanyam, a psychologist at California State University.

That bet — fame and wealth weighed against the risk of prison or worse — is one that Dalton Eatherly appears to have made.

To his thousands of followers he’s known as Chud the Builder. A self-described “America-first” influencer, he has garnered views by livestreaming confrontations with Black people, which often included racial slurs and harassment.

In May, one of Mr. Eatherly’s confrontational pursuits for clicks almost proved fatal.

A dispute with a man outside the Montgomery County Courthouse in Clarksville, Tenn., ended with gunfire as both men wielded firearms.

A video later surfaced of Mr. Eatherly on a stretcher with a microphone attached to his lapel.

Mr. Eatherly claimed self-defense but was later charged with several counts, including attempted murder. The case remains pending.

He and his lawyer could not be immediately reached for comment.

The social media platforms TikTok, Kick and YouTube (which is owned by Google’s parent company, Alphabet) and Facebook and Instagram (which are owned by Meta) said that they enforce community guidelines meant to restrict objectionable and dangerous content and that they ban users who violate their policies.

“To prevent copycat behavior, we prohibit people from facilitating, organizing, or promoting harmful activities,” a Meta representative said in a statement.

Experts who have studied digital behavior and online incentives said that boundary-pushing stunts are unlikely to ease as long as social media platforms reward such content.

“In many cases, that means escalating toward ever more extreme claims and risky behaviors that can endanger not only creators themselves but also their audiences, for whom it’s increasingly difficult to distinguish between what’s truly beneficial and what may be outright harmful,” said Jasmina Tacheva, an assistant professor at the School of Information Studies at Syracuse University.

Mr. Eatherly is not the only influencer to have courted danger.

In Loudoun County, Va., Sheriff Mike Chapman’s department responded to a call involving Tanner Cook, a YouTuber behind a channel called Classified Goons.

Mr. Cook, who is known for harassing unsuspecting strangers, repeatedly confronted a DoorDash driver inside the Dulles Town Center in Sterling, Va.

Mr. Cook shoved a phone into the driver’s face while a vulgar phrase played in a loop in what was an escalation of confrontational stunts he has filmed in other places.

The driver, Alan Colie, shot Mr. Cook, who survived.

A jury acquitted Mr. Colie of aggravated malicious wounding, finding that he acted in self-defense, but convicted him of discharging a firearm inside an occupied building.

After the verdict, Mr. Cook said the shooting would not change his approach.

“We are going to continue the videos and keep it pushing,” said Mr. Cook, whose YouTube channel has 66,000 subscribers. “It is what it is.”

Recent uploads show him streaming inside stores, falsely accusing a stranger of stealing and of him being thrown out of businesses. A video posted in early 2026 is titled “I almost got shot again!”

Mr. Cook and Mr. Colie did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

Sheriff Chapman’s office regularly warns residents about viral challenges and online trends. The pursuit of a laugh, he said, can carry real-world consequences.

“You may think this is funny,” Sheriff Chapman warned, “but this could end up as a disaster.”

The trend stretches beyond the United States.

The British government recently called on social media companies to remove more dangerous content, including videos of users filming themselves driving dangerously, after a string of deadly crashes that were linked to online stunts.

A press officer for Ofcom, the government’s regulator of communications services, said it opened an investigation into TikTok’s compliance with its child-safety responsibilities in July.

“Online content which encourages dangerous behavior and treats it as entertainment is totally unacceptable, and can have tragic and heartbreaking consequences,” the official said in a statement.

A TikTok representative said content that promotes dangerous behavior or could lead to serious injury violates its community guidelines, which prohibit criminal behavior, hate speech, and physical or sexual abuse, among other categories.

The platform has been redirecting videos of dangerous challenges to a safety center page. Violators can also be permanently banned, the representative said.

In France, Raphaël Graven, an internet personality who routinely subjected himself to acts of violence and verbal humiliation for an audience, died last year during a live broadcast on the platform Kick.

Some bruises on Mr. Graven’s body were found during an autopsy but none that could explain his death, French officials said.

The two men who ran the livestream channel, Owen Cenazandotti and Safine Hamadi, were not accused of causing the death but were convicted in August of aggravated violence, incitement to hatred and violence online. Both received suspended prison terms and were fined.

In a statement, Kick cited its community guidelines and terms of service, saying that users “must comply with all laws and regulations in their country” and that violators could have their content removed, be suspended or banned.

The company’s rules prohibit extreme violence, depictions of self-harm, graphic gore as well as content that puts personal safety at risk.

Kick said it moderates livestreams while considering “the full context” to evaluate potential violations.

Today, Mr. Jacob reflects on the lessons he learned from his plane crash stunt.

“I don’t regret what I did because it’s taught me a massive life lesson, and I’ve become somebody that I never otherwise would have become,” he said. “But that doesn’t mean that it was OK, and that I didn’t make a terrible decision.”

Looking back, he said there were other motivations, including money, curiosity and a desire to make a spectacular feat a reality. But attention was always part of the calculation.

He decided then that the risk was worth taking. Federal authorities and YouTube concluded otherwise.

“We have clear policies prohibiting extremely dangerous challenges, dangerous or threatening pranks, and other harmful or dangerous acts,” a YouTube representative said in a statement. “For example, the plane crash video was removed and the creator was suspended from the YouTube Partner Program after the incident.”

Prosecutors later said that Mr. Jacob intentionally destroyed evidence by removing the wreckage and lying to investigators about its location.

Mr. Jacob, who pleaded guilty to one federal count of destruction and concealment and served a little over four months of a six-month prison sentence, said that the legal case consumed roughly five years.

The consequences stretched far beyond the courtroom.

“It completely decimated my entire life,” he said. “I was homeless. I lost all my money. It’s been a hell of a climb out of hell.”

For younger viewers, the rewards from creating a spectacle — which come in the form of comments and views — may leave a strong impression, tempting them to perform their own dangerous act.

Often, experts said, younger viewers give little thought to the consequences.

“When you’re younger, you’re thinking less about the possible outcomes,” said Anton Ivanov, an assistant professor of information systems at the Gies College of Business at the University of Illinois. “You’re more interested in the immediate results.”

Susan C. Beachy and Sheelagh McNeill contributed research.

]]>

item.title: Ohio Republican in Key Senate Race Fires Campaign Aide, Citing Social Media Photo of Nazis
item.description:
The campaign of Senator Jon Husted, Republican of Ohio, said that it had fired its political director after learning that he once posted a photo of Nazi soldiers as his profile picture on Facebook.

The political director, Stephen B. Woytek, 25, was named in August to his role working for Mr. Husted, who is running in one of a handful of competitive races that could determine control of the Senate in November. Amy Natoce, a spokeswoman for the Husted campaign, said in a statement on Friday that Mr. Woytek’s social media use showed a “complete lack” of judgment and a “disregard for its impact on others.” She added that “upon learning about” Mr. Woytek’s “social media posts” on Friday, Mr. Husted “made the immediate decision to part ways.”

The Washington Post first reported on Friday that Mr. Woytek in 2018 used a photo of SS soldiers as his Facebook profile picture. Ms. Natoce confirmed Saturday that her statement referred to that photo. The Post also reported that Mr. Woytek recently added to a public playlist of songs on Spotify celebrating Rhodesia, the white-minority-ruled African colony that became Zimbabwe and has been frequently celebrated by white-supremacist groups.

The New York Times has not independently confirmed that social media activity. The Post reported that after it contacted Mr. Husted’s campaign, the campaign said it was parting ways with Mr. Woytek.

Mr. Woytek did not respond to requests for comment. In a statement to The Post, he said that he participated in historical re-enactments and should have “exercised better judgment when posting about my activities online.” He said he rejected “the racist and antisemitic ideology the SS and Nazi Germany represented.”

Some of Mr. Woytek’s social media accounts and posts appeared to be set as private or deleted as of Saturday morning.

Ms. Natoce said in her statement that Mr. Woytek, a graduate of the Citadel, “serves our country honorably as a lieutenant in the U.S. Army” and “studies military history and routinely reenacts historical battles.” She said Mr. Woytek “denies negative intent.”

In 2018, Mr. Woytek featured a photo of SS soldiers holding captured Soviet banners as his profile picture on Facebook, The Post reported.

Mr. Woytek also participated in Civil War re-enactments as a Union soldier, according to Mr. Husted’s campaign.

Ms. Natoce did not respond to inquiries about the campaign’s initial vetting of Mr. Woytek and whether it examined his social media history.

“You have our statement,” Ms. Natoce said in a text message. “That’s all I will be saying on the matter.”

Mr. Husted faces a challenge from former Senator Sherrod Brown, a Democrat who lost his seat in 2024.

A spokeswoman for Mr. Brown, Lauren Chou, criticized Mr. Husted over the episode. “They say you are the company you keep,” Ms. Chou said in a statement, adding that “Ohioans deserve a leader who reflects their values.”

Mr. Husted and Mr. Brown are competing to serve the remainder of Vice President JD Vance’s Senate term, which ends after 2028. Mr. Husted was appointed in early 2025 to replace Mr. Vance.

item.title: A Mastodon Tooth From the Ice Age Is Discovered in a California Creek
item.description:
Brigid Lynch, a geologist, was conducting a field survey for a frog habitat near a San Mateo County, Calif., creek on a morning in March when something caught her eye.

“I looked down and was kind of like, ‘That’s really weird looking,’” she recalled. “‘What is that?’”

She alerted her colleague, Jeneya Fertel, and they both stared at it.

“I was like, ‘Do you think we should touch it?’” Ms. Lynch recalled. She thought it might be a living thing, so she said to Mr. Fertel, “You pick it up.”

They assessed that it was a little bigger than a toaster oven and weighed maybe three or four pounds. They put it back, and forgot about it.

Ms. Lynch continued her field work and the next day noticed the oddity again while going through her photos.

She ran her photo through a reverse-image search on Google and was shocked by what she had found.

“This is absolutely a Pacific mastodon molar,” she recalled thinking.

The Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District, a public agency known as Midpen that has preserved more than 70,000 acres of open space in the Bay Area, announced the discovery on Wednesday.

After leaving the molar in the creek, Ms. Lynch contacted colleagues at the environmental consulting firm Balance Hydrologics to properly retrieve the fossil.

Wayne Thompson, a paleontologist since 1976 and owner of Pacific Paleontology, confirmed the find as a Pacific mastodon molar and suggested ways to relocate it.

“I helped them store it in a way that would not deteriorate the molar because once molars are removed from a watery environment, they start decaying rapidly,” he said.

Staff members at Midpen were able to keep the molar stored in a bucket of creek water.

In its news release, Midpen said it donated the fossilized tooth to the Doerr School of Sustainability at Stanford University, where researchers plan to determine its age through carbon dating and to create a 3-D scan of it.

Mr. Thompson said the Pacific mastodon is distinct from American mastodons because of their narrower teeth and thicker leg bones.

In 2019, researchers published a study with the U.S. Geological Survey naming the Pacific mastodon (Mammut pacificus) as a newly recognized species of mastodon.

Pacific mastodons lived during the Pleistocene Epoch, or the Ice Age, which began roughly 2.5 million years ago. They disappeared about 11,700 years ago.

Mr. Thompson said the shape of a Pacific mastodon’s molar is distinct because the creatures were herbivores that used their cone-shaped teeth to browse trees and grind leaves and small twigs.

“So you can think of a proboscidean, whether it’s an elephant or a mammoth or a mastodon, as having teeth that are on conveyor belts,” he said. “And they come in from the back of the jaw and they migrate inside the jaw up front and then they erupt and then they continue on the conveyor belt moving forward until they’re ejected.”

Mr. Thompson believes this particular Pacific mastodon lived to be around 35 or 40 years old, and that the molar may have only “recently” detached from the jawbone.

Mr. Thompson called the find “a really unique discovery” and said that the remains of Pacific mastodons are rare in the area and are more commonly found in Southern California.

“This mastodon discovery really gives us a lot of information in terms of where these creatures were living,” he said.

Georgia Gee contributed research Jackeline Luna contributed reporting.
